title.title: Build & Integration
title.subtitle: How a smart contract actually gets built and deployed: a standard, a template, a tool, a testnet.

why.heading: You have designed the contract. How does it actually go live?
why.subtitle: Four moves take a contract from a whiteboard to a public blockchain. This section walks them in order.

start.label: Designed
start.desc: Sections 1–5: you know what it should do, and whether it deserves a chain.

end.label: Live
end.desc: A public address that anyone can call.

steps.label: Standard
steps.desc: Build to a shape the ecosystem already supports: an ERC.

steps.label: Template
steps.desc: Start from vetted OpenZeppelin code instead of a blank page.

steps.label: Tool & network
steps.desc: Pick where you write it and which chain it lands on.

steps.label: Deploy
steps.desc: Put it on a testnet yourself and send it one transaction.

why.bridge: Coming up: a hands-on assignment where you prompt an AI for a contract and deploy it to a testnet yourself. These slides are the map.

erc.heading: ERC standards: build to the shape everyone already supports
erc.subtitle: An ERC (Ethereum Request for Comments) is a published interface: a fixed list of functions and events. Follow it, and wallets, exchanges and marketplaces can talk to your contract from day one.
erc.evolveBody: anyone can propose one through the open EIP process. ERC-721 had no way to describe royalties, so ERC-2981 added it.
erc.noEvents: No events required by this standard

erc-20.purpose: Cryptocurrencies, DeFi tokens, governance tokens, stablecoins.
erc-20.takeaway: The "standard money" of Ethereum: every wallet and exchange supports it.

erc-721.purpose: Unique digital items: art, collectibles, tickets, in-game assets, real-estate deeds.
erc-721.takeaway: Enables NFTs: one-of-a-kind, ownable digital assets.
erc-721.examples: BAYC · ENS names · Uniswap v3 positions · Propy real-estate deeds

erc-1155.purpose: Fungible and non-fungible tokens in a single contract; built for batch transfers.
erc-1155.takeaway: One contract, many token types. Batch transfers save gas. Common in gaming.
erc-1155.examples: Game items · event tickets · limited editions

erc-2981.purpose: Tell NFT marketplaces, in a standard way, who should receive a royalty and how much.
erc-2981.takeaway: Fills a gap in ERC-721. It only reports the royalty: paying it is still up to the marketplace.
erc-2981.examples: Read by NFT marketplaces such as OpenSea and Rarible

eip.heading: How an EIP becomes a standard
eip.subtitle: Why care: nobody owns ERC-20. A standard starts as an EIP (Ethereum Improvement Proposal) that anyone can write.
eip.zoomLabel: Zoomed out: who moves a proposal forward

actors.label: Proposer
actors.desc: Writes the EIP and builds consensus for it

actors.label: EIP editors
actors.desc: Check the form, not the merit of the idea

actors.label: Community
actors.desc: Developers, wallets and node teams review it in public

actors.label: Final standard
actors.desc: Frozen text that everyone can build on

eip.hint: Click a status, or use the button to advance

idea.tagline: an idea, not yet a document
idea.what: You have an idea for a standard. Before writing anything formal you test it in public, usually in a thread on the Ethereum Magicians forum: is it original, and does anyone need it?
idea.rule: Not tracked in the EIP repository yet: no number, no status.

draft.who: The proposer, then an EIP editor.
draft.what: You write the proposal in the official template and open a pull request on GitHub. An EIP editor checks that it is complete and properly formatted, assigns it a number and merges it.
draft.rule: The first formally tracked stage. Editors do the administrative and editorial part: they do not pass judgment on the idea.

review.what: You mark the EIP as ready for peer review. Developers, wallet teams and auditors pick it apart in the open, and the text keeps changing in response.
review.rule: The author is responsible for building consensus and for documenting dissenting opinions.

lastCall.what: The final review window before Final. A deadline is published, typically 14 days out, so that anyone with a last objection can raise it.
lastCall.rule: If Last Call brings up a necessary change to the specification itself, the EIP goes back to Review.

final.what: The EIP is now the final standard. Its text is frozen: from here it is only updated to correct errata and add non-normative clarifications.
final.rule: An ERC is adopted by choice: wallets and apps decide to support it. A Core EIP has to be implemented in the node software and goes live in a network upgrade.

side.stagnant: Inactive for 6 months or more while in Draft, Review or Last Call. The authors or an editor can revive it by moving it back to Draft or to its earlier status.
side.withdrawn: The authors have withdrawn the proposal. This is final: it cannot be revived under the same number. If the idea comes back, it is a new proposal.
side.living: A special status for EIPs designed to be updated continually and never reach Final. The best-known example is EIP-1, the document that defines this process.

doc.forumPost: Idea: a standard way for NFT contracts to report royalties?
doc.forumMeta: Discussion open · no EIP number yet

eip.typesLabel: What kind of EIP? Click a type
eip.standardsTrackDesc: affects most or all Ethereum implementations

core.desc: Changes to the protocol itself. Most need a consensus fork: every node has to upgrade.
core.example: EIP-1559, the 2021 change to how transaction fees work.

networking.desc: How nodes talk to each other: the peer-to-peer network protocols.
networking.example: EIP-8, forward-compatibility rules for the node-to-node protocol.

interface.desc: Shared conventions at the interface level, such as method names and contract ABIs.
interface.example: EIP-1193, the standard way a website talks to a wallet such as MetaMask.

erc.desc: Application-level standards: tokens, name registries, wallet formats. Filed in their own repository, ethereum/ERCs.

meta.desc: Describes a process around Ethereum, or a change to one. It does not change the protocol.
meta.example: EIP-1, the rules of this very process.

informational.desc: Guidelines or information for the community. It proposes no new feature.
informational.example: EIP-2228, which settles the official name of the main network: "Ethereum Mainnet".

template.heading: Do not write it from scratch: remix a vetted template
template.subtitle: OpenZeppelin publishes open-source, audited implementations of the standards. You inherit one and add only what is yours.

parts.label: Import
parts.desc: One line pulls in OpenZeppelin's ERC-20: every function and event of the standard, already written and reviewed.

parts.label: Inherit
parts.desc: "is ERC20" makes your contract a standard token. Wallets and exchanges recognise it with no extra work.

parts.label: Yours
parts.desc: The only part you decide: the name, the symbol, and how many tokens exist at launch.

template.aiBody: ask it to remix this template, not to invent a token from scratch. Then read what it wrote before you deploy it.

ai.heading: AI-driven development: the AI drafts, you stay the author
ai.subtitle: Why it matters: you no longer need to write code to get a working contract, and the assignment asks you to do exactly that. But your wallet signs the deployment, so you have to understand every line.
ai.hint: Pick a prompt, copy it, paste it into any AI assistant

prompts.goal: get a first version built on the vetted template, with every line explained.
prompts.prompt: Write a minimal ERC-20 token in Solidity named ClassToken (symbol CLS) with a fixed supply of 1,000,000 tokens, all minted to the deployer. Inherit OpenZeppelin Contracts v5: do not rewrite ERC-20 yourself. No owner, no mint function, no extra features. Add a comment in plain English explaining each line for a non-programmer. Then list the steps to deploy it on the Sepolia testnet with Remix and a phone wallet (Rabby or Zerion).
checks: It imports OpenZeppelin instead of rewriting ERC-20 by hand.
It compiles in Remix with no changes.
You can say in your own words what each line does.

prompts.goal: understand a contract you did not write, including one an AI has just handed you.
prompts.prompt:
Explain what this Solidity contract does in plain English, one function at a time. For each function tell me: who is allowed to call it, what it changes, and whether it can create, move or destroy tokens. Is there an owner or admin with special powers?

[paste the contract here]
checks: The explanation matches what you asked for in prompt 1.
No function shows up that you did not ask for.
Ask a second AI the same question and compare the answers.

prompts.goal: get a second opinion before you deploy.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a smart-contract security reviewer. Is the contract below safe to deploy on a testnet? List anything risky or unusual: unlimited minting, owner-only powers, external calls, anything that differs from the standard OpenZeppelin ERC-20. For each point say why it matters and how to fix it. If you are not sure about something, say so instead of guessing.

[paste the contract here]
checks: An AI review is a second opinion, not an audit.
Models miss real bugs and invent fake ones: check each claim against the code.
Anything that will hold real money needs a professional audit.

tools.label: Chat assistants
tools.desc: Paste a prompt, get the contract and the explanation. The easiest place to start.

tools.label: Coding agents
tools.desc: Work inside a code editor: they create the files, compile, and can write and run tests.

tools.label: RemixAI Assistant
tools.desc: Built into Remix, where you deploy. It writes a contract from a description, explains a contract, and explains compiler errors.

tools.label: OpenZeppelin Wizard & MCP
tools.desc: The Wizard builds a standard contract from tick-boxes, with no AI: a baseline to compare against. The MCP server lets AI agents generate from the same vetted templates.

loop.label: Read
loop.desc: Until you can explain it yourself

loop.label: Test
loop.desc: On a testnet: mistakes are free

ai.secretWarning: Never paste a recovery phrase or private key into an AI or a website. Prompts may be stored by the provider.

where.heading: Pick a tool and a network
where.subtitle: Same contract, same steps. Only the stakes change.

learn.name: Remix
learn.desc: An IDE in your browser. Write, compile and deploy from one tab. Nothing to install.

real.name: Hardhat or Foundry
real.desc: A project on your own machine, with automated tests and scripted, repeatable deployments.

learn.name: Sepolia testnet
learn.desc: A public Ethereum test network. It behaves like the real chain, so the steps you learn carry over.

real.name: Ethereum mainnet or a Layer 2
real.desc: Layer 2s such as Arbitrum or Base run the same Solidity code, usually at lower fees.

learn.name: Nothing
learn.desc: Gas is paid in free test ETH from a faucet. It has no real value, so a mistake costs nothing.

real.name: Real money
real.desc: Gas costs real ETH and the contract may hold real funds. Deployed code cannot simply be edited: test and audit first.

ladder.label: Sandbox
ladder.desc: Remix VM: a private chain inside your browser tab

ladder.label: Public testnet
ladder.desc: Sepolia: a real network, play money

deploy.heading: Deploy to a testnet: wallet → testnet → deploy → one transaction
deploy.subtitle: Four steps, a few minutes, zero real money. Click through them.

steps.label: Wallet
steps.title: Create a wallet
actions: On your phone, install [Rabby (rabby.io)](https://rabby.io) or [Zerion (zerion.io)](https://zerion.io) from the App Store or Google Play, then create an account.
Write the secret recovery phrase down on paper. Never share it, never type it into a website.
Use a fresh wallet for testing, not one that holds real funds.
steps.bridge: you generated a key pair. The address is public; the phrase is the key. This is the identity that will sign everything that follows.

steps.label: Testnet
steps.title: Switch to the testnet and get test ETH
actions: In the wallet, switch the network to Sepolia (turn on test networks, or add Sepolia as a custom network, if it is hidden).
Copy your address into a Sepolia faucet and request test ETH.
Wait for the balance to appear. That is your gas money.
steps.bridge: even a test network charges gas. Test ETH pays for it exactly like real ETH, but it is free and has no real value.

steps.label: Deploy
steps.title: Deploy the contract
actions: Open Remix, paste the contract and press Compile.
In Deploy & Run, set the environment to WalletConnect and scan the QR code with your phone wallet.
Press Deploy and confirm on your phone. Seconds later the contract has an address.
steps.bridge: deploying is itself a transaction. You signed it, the network stored your code, and that code now lives at a permanent public address.

steps.label: One transaction
steps.title: Send it one transaction
actions: In Remix, open the deployed contract and call a function, for example transfer 10 tokens to a classmate.
Confirm in the wallet: you sign, and you pay gas.
Look the transaction hash up on the block explorer.
steps.bridge: trigger, execute, update, emit: the Section 02 workflow, this time run by you. The explorer page is public proof that it happened.

mock.phraseNote: 12 words. Whoever has them controls the wallet.
mock.addressNote: public, safe to share. It is how others pay you and how a faucet finds you.
mock.faucetNote: A faucet is a website that gives away small amounts of test ETH.
mock.unitsNote: Amounts are in the smallest unit: 10 MTK is 10 followed by 18 zeros.

hosting.heading: Node infrastructure and where to host
hosting.subtitle: Why it matters: your contract is live, but people need a website to click on, and that website has to reach the chain. Three pieces, three jobs: a host serves the site, RPC reads the chain, the wallet changes it.

load.label: Open the site
load.desc: The browser downloads your site's files from the static host. No blockchain is involved yet: it is an ordinary website.

read.label: Read from the chain
read.desc: The site asks an RPC provider a question, such as "what is this balance?", and the provider's node answers. Free, near-instant, nothing to sign, and nothing on the chain changes.

write.label: Send a transaction
write.desc: The site asks the wallet to send a transaction. The user confirms, the wallet signs it and sends it to the network. This is the only way anything on the chain changes, and it costs gas.

zones.front: Front end: a static site you host
zones.chain: Chain access: RPC to read, the wallet to write

host.label: Static host
host.desc: Stores your site's files and serves them to any visitor.

browser.label: The user's browser
browser.desc: Runs your site. This is the app people actually see.

wallet.label: Wallet
wallet.desc: Holds the user's keys. Signs each transaction and sends it to the network.

rpc.label: RPC provider
rpc.desc: Read access to a node. Your site asks it what is on the chain.

chain.label: Ethereum network
chain.desc: Many independent nodes. Each one already holds a copy of your contract.

front.title: Where does the front end live?
front.lead: A dapp front end is just files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), so any static host will do.

options.name: GitHub Pages
options.desc: Publishes a website straight from a GitHub repository.

options.name: Cloudflare Pages
options.desc: Connect a repository: each push redeploys the site on Cloudflare's global network.

front.also: Same idea: Vercel, Netlify. A free plan is usually enough for a class project.

chain.title: How does it reach the chain?
chain.lead: Two doors: you read through an RPC provider, and you change things through the user's wallet.

options.name: Read · RPC provider
options.desc: Infura, Alchemy and others run the node. You get an API key.

options.name: Read · your own node
options.desc: Same read access, no middleman. You pay in storage and upkeep.

options.name: Write · the user's wallet
options.desc: Rabby, Zerion and others. The user signs and sends; your site never holds keys.

chain.tradeoff: Trade-off: a provider saves you the work, but puts one company between your site and the chain.

events.heading: Event-driven architecture: the contract announces, your app reacts
events.subtitle: Why it matters: a contract cannot send an email, refresh a screen or call your CRM. All it can do is announce that something happened. An event is that announcement, and it is the trigger your off-chain systems wait for.
events.hint: Pick a situation, then send the transaction

payment.label: A customer pays in tokens
reactions: Order marked as paid, shipping starts

delivery.label: A delivery is confirmed
reactions: Buyer told that the parcel has arrived
ERP releases the supplier invoice for payment

ticket.label: An NFT ticket is minted
reactions: Ticket and QR code emailed to the buyer
Buyer added to the guest list in the CRM

events.eventNote: Written to the transaction's log, where anyone can read it.
events.listenerNote: the whole listener, in one line (ethers.js)

facts.label: A log entry, not a message
facts.desc: The contract does not call anyone. It writes the event to the transaction log, and whoever is listening picks it up.

facts.label: One-way
facts.desc: Contracts cannot read events, not even their own. Events exist for the outside world.

facts.label: Live or later
facts.desc: An app can subscribe through a node and get events as they happen, or search past ones at any time.

events.fitBody: the listener reaches the chain through the same node access as on the previous slide. This is how your existing systems keep in step with the contract without anyone watching a block explorer.

deeper.heading: Going deeper: the stack around a live contract
deeper.subtitle: A deployed contract is one piece. A real product wraps ordinary software around it. Skim this now and come back when you build.

spine.label: Your app
spine.desc: The website or back-office system people actually use.

spine.label: Library
spine.desc: Turns a button click into a transaction for the wallet to sign.

spine.label: Node access
spine.desc: The doorway to the network: a provider, or a node you run yourself.

spine.label: Your contract
spine.desc: The code you deployed, at its permanent address.

around.label: Oracles
around.desc: Bring outside facts on-chain. The contract is only as safe as that data.

around.label: Events
around.desc: The contract emits an event; your systems listen and react, like a webhook.

around.label: Off-chain data
around.desc: Large or private data stays off-chain. The chain keeps only a hash that proves it.

around.label: AI tools
around.desc: Fast for drafts, documentation and prototypes. Not a substitute for review and an audit.

keyPoints.s6-why: Shipping a contract is a short, repeatable routine: standard, template, tool, testnet.
keyPoints.s6-erc: A standard is a promise about your contract's buttons, so tools built by strangers work with it.
keyPoints.s6-eip: A standard is not decreed. Anyone can propose it, editors check its form, and open review makes it Final.
keyPoints.s6-template: The safest line of code is the one you did not have to write.
keyPoints.s6-ai: AI can write the contract. Only you can answer for it: if you cannot explain a line, do not deploy it.
keyPoints.s6-where: A testnet is a dress rehearsal: same tools, same steps, nothing at stake.
keyPoints.s6-deploy: Do these four steps once on a testnet and you know the routine: mainnet is the same, with real money.
keyPoints.s6-hosting: The host serves the site, an RPC provider reads the chain, the wallet writes to it. The contract itself is already hosted, by the network.
keyPoints.s6-events: A contract cannot reach out to your systems. It emits an event, and everything off-chain is a reaction to it.
keyPoints.s6-deeper: The contract is the smallest part of the product. Everything around it is ordinary software.

takeaways.title: Section 06 — Key Takeaways
items: Shipping a contract is a routine: pick a standard, remix a template, choose a tool and a network, deploy
An ERC is a shared interface, agreed in the open through the EIP process: follow one and wallets, exchanges and marketplaces work with your contract from day one
Do not write from scratch: inherit OpenZeppelin's audited contracts and add only your own rules
Rehearse on a testnet such as Sepolia: the same steps as mainnet, paid in free test ETH. You end with a public contract address and a transaction hash anyone can check
Around the contract: a static site for the front end, an RPC provider to read the chain, the user's wallet to sign transactions, and events that tell your other systems what happened
AI can draft the code. You still read it, test it on a testnet, and have anything that holds real money audited

quizTemplate.question: Your team needs a loyalty-points token for a pilot. What is the most sensible way to build the contract?
options: Write every function yourselves, so that no outside code is involved.
Inherit OpenZeppelin's audited ERC-20 and add only your own rules on top.
Design your own token interface, so wallets and exchanges have to integrate with you.
Skip the standard: ERC standards only matter for NFTs.
quizTemplate.explanation: ERC-20 is the interface wallets and exchanges already understand, and OpenZeppelin's implementation has been reviewed and used far more than anything a team writes in a week. Inheriting it leaves you with a few lines of your own to get right. Writing it all yourself adds risk for no benefit, a custom interface throws away compatibility, and ERC-20 is itself a token standard that has nothing to do with NFTs.

quizTestnet.question: Why deploy to a testnet such as Sepolia before going to mainnet?
options: A testnet is private, so competitors cannot see your code.
A contract that works on a testnet is copied to mainnet automatically.
Ethereum requires every contract to spend time on a testnet first.
The tools and steps are the same, but the ETH is free and worthless, so mistakes cost nothing.
quizTestnet.explanation: A public testnet behaves like mainnet and uses the same wallet, tools and steps, but gas is paid in test ETH that has no real value. That makes it the place to make your mistakes. Testnets are public, not private. Nothing moves to mainnet automatically: going live is a separate deployment that you pay for in real ETH. And no rule forces you to use a testnet; it is simply good practice.

quiz.question: Your team is building a tokenized real-estate platform. You need: (a) standard ERC-20 and ERC-721 tokens, (b) low fees, because rent is distributed often, (c) to reuse audited OpenZeppelin contracts. Which platform fits BEST?
options: Hyperledger Fabric: permissioned, enterprise-grade, no gas fees.
Solana: high throughput, low cost, fast finality.
An EVM-compatible Layer 2 such as Arbitrum or Base: the same Solidity code and ERC standards as Ethereum, at lower fees.
Cardano: a focus on formal verification, with its own contract languages.
quiz.explanation: All three requirements point to the EVM. ERC standards and OpenZeppelin's contracts are written in Solidity for EVM chains, and a Layer 2 runs that same code while charging lower fees than Ethereum mainnet. Fabric, Solana and Cardano are capable platforms, but none of them runs Solidity ERC contracts natively: you would be rebuilding the standards and giving up the audited code you wanted to reuse.
